metadata.assigned_reading: Bank for International Settlements, The Future Monetary System, Annual Economic Report 2022, Chapter 3

questions.question_stem: A government is less worried that citizens are using a new unit of account and more worried that dollar-denominated payments are moving outside banks it can supervise. Which lesson framework best explains the concern?
questions.correct_answer: The payment infrastructure layer is being challenged because an existing currency is moving over rails the state does not fully control.
incorrect_answers: The currency layer is being replaced because any sovereign unit of account is shifting onto domestic banking rails the state operates.
The consensus mechanism is being bypassed because a cryptographic asset is migrating over ledgers the central bank actively monitors.
The inclusion layer is being undermined because an algorithmic stablecoin is trading over networks the public has actively rejected.
questions.explanation: The lesson separates the currency layer from the payment infrastructure layer. Stablecoins can preserve the familiar sovereign unit of account while shifting transfer activity onto non-bank or public-chain rails.
questions.lesson_block: Currency Layer vs Payment Infrastructure Layer
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/conclusion_02-AS-cbdcs_stablecoins-slides-only.qmd#Taxonomy Of Digital Money / Government Motives And The Permission-Layer Framework

questions.question_stem: Which design feature most clearly distinguishes a CBDC from a permissionless cryptocurrency in the lesson's trust-architecture comparison?
questions.correct_answer: A CBDC uses a hierarchy of authorized issuers, intermediaries, credentials, and revocation powers rather than open self-generated participation.
incorrect_answers: A CBDC uses a network of anonymous validators, consensus rules, cryptographic proofs, and fork choices rather than managed retail credentials.
A CBDC relies upon synchronized copies, public ledgers, zero-knowledge proofs, and automated smart contracts rather than sovereign authority.
A CBDC operates with decentralized nodes, collateral pools, algorithmic pegs, and liquidity links rather than central sovereign liabilities.
questions.explanation: The lesson frames CBDCs as state liabilities on permissioned infrastructure. Their trust model depends on controlled issuance, credentialed participation, and authority to revoke, freeze, or reverse at defined control points.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/conclusion_02-AS-cbdcs_stablecoins-slides-only.qmd#Trust Architecture And Permission / Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs)

questions.question_stem: A stablecoin issuer can blacklist a known address, but users can still create new wallets and broadcast transfers on the underlying public chain. What does this illustrate?
questions.correct_answer: Issuer-level controls can exist alongside network-level openness, so freezing known addresses is not the same as permissioning the whole transfer network.
incorrect_answers: Issuer-level freezes automatically require validator approval, so blacklisting one wallet means permissioning all public-chain transfers everywhere by design.
Network-level openness disappears once an issuer can freeze tokens, so every new wallet must be preapproved by the stablecoin company before transfers begin.
Address blacklists prove the underlying blockchain is permissioned, so users cannot broadcast transactions unless the token issuer signs them first directly.
questions.explanation: Stablecoins combine centralized issuer powers with potentially permissionless network transfer. The issuer may freeze or redeem at its layer without controlling every wallet, validator, or peer-to-peer transaction path.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/conclusion_02-AS-cbdcs_stablecoins-slides-only.qmd#Stablecoin Hybrid Trust / Case Study: USDT On Tron

questions.question_stem: A bank loses access to SWIFT but still has potential paths to settle value through correspondent accounts or alternative rails. What misconception does this scenario target?
questions.correct_answer: SWIFT is primarily a messaging system, while final movement of value depends on settlement systems and banking relationships.
incorrect_answers: SWIFT is mainly a settlement ledger, while final verification of messages depends on automated oracle feeds and consensus nodes.
SWIFT is a wallet application, while final distribution of liquidity depends on retail transfers and collateralized token pegs.
SWIFT is a central-bank clearinghouse, while final settlement depends on its direct control over correspondent bank accounts globally.
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes payment instructions from settlement. SWIFT messaging can be a major chokepoint, but dollar settlement, correspondent banking, Fedwire, CHIPS, and alternatives represent related but distinct control surfaces.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/conclusion_02-AS-cbdcs_stablecoins-slides-only.qmd#Payment Rails As State Power / Messaging vs Settlement

questions.question_stem: Why are dollar stablecoins strategically contested even when they do not introduce a new sovereign currency?
questions.correct_answer: They can make dollar-denominated value transferable outside conventional dollar banking rails and outside some state permission gates.
incorrect_answers: They can convert dollar units into new sovereign money outside foreign-exchange markets and outside every commercial bank ledger system.
They can make central-bank reserves spendable by retail wallets outside wholesale accounts and outside normal reserve access rules instantly.
They can remove dollar pegs from issuer liabilities outside collateral management and outside any redemption obligations entirely for users.
questions.explanation: The lesson argues that stablecoins more immediately challenge payment infrastructure than the currency unit. They can carry sovereign-denominated value, especially dollars, over networks governments do not fully operate.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/conclusion_02-AS-cbdcs_stablecoins-slides-only.qmd#Stablecoins As The Contested Middle / The Permission Layer

questions.question_stem: A student says all stablecoins have the same risk profile because they all try to trade near one dollar. Which response best follows the lesson?
questions.correct_answer: Stablecoins can rely on different collateral and governance models, so redemption risk, transparency, peg maintenance, and enforcement surfaces can differ.
incorrect_answers: Stablecoins can rely on automated contract and oracle structures, so transaction fees, settlement speeds, validator counts, and consensus systems are uniform.
Stablecoins must utilize identical regulatory licensing frameworks, so state oversight, audit access, capital reserves, and seizure powers are identical.
Stablecoins can operate through permissioned consortium and validators, so hardware setups, network bandwidth, latency, and mining outcomes are static.
questions.explanation: The lesson compares fiat-backed, crypto-backed, and algorithmic designs as different mechanisms with different trust assumptions, reserve questions, transparency issues, and regulatory exposure.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/conclusion_02-AS-cbdcs_stablecoins-slides-only.qmd#Stablecoin Collateral Models / Stablecoins: Types and Mechanisms

questions.question_stem: Which government objective most directly explains why a state might pursue a CBDC rather than simply tolerate private stablecoin growth?
questions.correct_answer: It wants to modernize digital payments while preserving state control over issuance, participation, compliance, and monetary infrastructure.
incorrect_answers: It wants to outsource financial oversight while granting private entities control over minting, blacklisting, auditing, and reserve management.
It wants to eliminate transaction friction while transferring validator control over consensus, mining, governance, and cryptographic checks.
It wants to automate commercial assets while delegating systemic leverage over settlement, rates, liquidity, and correspondent networks.
questions.explanation: The lesson presents CBDCs as state efforts to own both money and rails. Governments may pursue them for modernization, inclusion, sovereignty, sanctions enforcement, and capital-flow control.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/conclusion_02-AS-cbdcs_stablecoins-slides-only.qmd#Government Motives And The Permission-Layer Framework / Why Governments Care

questions.question_stem: In an economy with high inflation, strict capital controls, and limited access to dollar banking, why might USDT on Tron become useful even if it creates enforcement concerns?
questions.correct_answer: It can provide low-friction access to dollar-denominated payments over open network rails, while local authorities may struggle to control every wallet-level transfer.
incorrect_answers: It can offer high-latency settlement to gold-backed accounts over permissioned ledger systems, while local state authorities can easily audit every legal-entity exchange.
It can enforce real-name identification to commercial-bank assets over regulated central databases, while local authorities can supervise every peer-to-peer balance.
It can eliminate issuer-level supervision to algorithmic reserves over private oracle networks, while local authorities must authorize every validator-level block.
questions.explanation: The USDT-on-Tron case illustrates de facto dollar infrastructure: users may value dollar-denominated transfer on low-cost public rails, while issuer-level controls and network-level openness remain separate.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/conclusion_02-AS-cbdcs_stablecoins-slides-only.qmd#Case Study: USDT On Tron / De Facto Dollar Infrastructure

questions.question_stem: A cross-border CBDC pilot demonstrates fast settlement between several central banks. Why does the lesson warn against treating that result as proof of mature global adoption?
questions.correct_answer: Technical settlement progress does not resolve governance, membership rules, compliance, data visibility, dispute handling, or policy coordination at global scale.
incorrect_answers: Automated protocol upgrades do not guarantee decentralization, crypto safety, validator rewards, hash rates, censorship resistance, or user privacy at national scale.
Physical ledger distribution does not eliminate network fees, settlement delays, reserve inflation, commercial margins, or clearing networks at a regional scale.
Sovereign currency issuance does not require reserve backing, firm compliance, legal tender, balance sheets, capital controls, or inclusion at any local scale.
questions.explanation: The mBridge discussion separates technical feasibility from governance scalability. A working prototype or MVP can be important without proving broad production readiness or international policy alignment.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/conclusion_02-AS-cbdcs_stablecoins-slides-only.qmd#mBridge: A Test Case / mBridge So Far

questions.question_stem: Which comparison best applies the lesson's three-way permission-layer framework?
questions.correct_answer: Cryptocurrencies challenge state currency at the protocol layer, stablecoins move sovereign units over non-state rails, and CBDCs try to keep both money and rails under state authority.
incorrect_answers: Traditional commercial banks control retail transactions at the user interface layer, standard credit cards process payments, and stablecoins try to bypass reserves under federal mandates.
Central banks automate sovereign domestic reserves at the balance layer, traditional fiat assets settle over local clearing, and cryptocurrencies try to remove records under networks.
Consensus protocols enforce rewards at the validator layer, contracts run logic over public networks, and private nodes try to hold both assets and identity under corporate control.
questions.explanation: The lesson's comparison is direct: Bitcoin and Ethereum challenge the currency layer, stablecoins challenge infrastructure by carrying familiar units on alternate rails, and CBDCs are the state-led attempt to control both layers.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/conclusion_02-AS-cbdcs_stablecoins-slides-only.qmd#The Permission Layer: Three Challenges to State Control

questions.question_stem: The BIS reading argues that stablecoins expose crypto's need for a nominal anchor. What does that mean?
questions.correct_answer: Their usefulness depends on pegging to an existing sovereign unit of account rather than creating an independent, widely stable monetary unit.
incorrect_answers: Their overall security depends on linking to a state validator pool rather than creating a decentralized, mathematically secure consensus system.
Their efficiency depends on migrating to a rapid execution ledger rather than developing an interoperable, globally stable settlement layer.
The legal status depends on registering with a domestic regulatory agency rather than operating an anonymous, permissionless payment rail.
questions.explanation: The reading says stablecoins import credibility from sovereign money. A dollar-pegged token is useful partly because users want the dollar's unit of account, not because crypto has solved monetary stability on its own.
questions.specific_source_reading: /tmp/blockchain-course-readings/text/bis_future_monetary_system.txt#Stablecoins As Imported Credibility / Stablecoins in search of a nominal anchor

questions.question_stem: According to the BIS reading, why are permissionless crypto scalability problems not merely a matter of waiting for faster hardware?
questions.correct_answer: Validator incentives, congestion fees, security tradeoffs, and migration to new chains create structural pressure toward fragmentation.
incorrect_answers: Hardware latency, network bandwidth, storage limits, and ongoing processing delays create physical constraints toward centralization.
Consensus protocols, external oracle inputs, smart contracts, and liquidity bridges create automated reliance toward intermediation.
Regulatory compliance, capital limits, reserve audits, and local licensing rules create political obstacles toward standardization.
questions.explanation: The reading frames congestion and fragmentation as incentive and governance problems. Attempts to escape high fees or low throughput can produce new chains, weaker security assumptions, and bridge risks.
questions.specific_source_reading: /tmp/blockchain-course-readings/text/bis_future_monetary_system.txt#Permissionless Blockchains, Incentives, And Fragmentation / Structural limitations of crypto

questions.question_stem: A country launches a real-time retail payment system that lets users send bank deposits instantly through regulated payment providers, but users do not hold direct central bank liabilities. How would the BIS reading classify the distinction from a retail CBDC?
questions.correct_answer: It can modernize payments like a retail fast payment system, but it differs from a retail CBDC because the user's claim is on private intermediaries rather than directly on the central bank.
incorrect_answers: It can settle transactions like an algorithmic stablecoin, but it differs from a collateralized token because the user's own asset is on decentralized ledgers rather than on the issuer balance.
It can support financial inclusion like a permissionless token, but it differs from public networks because the user's identity is on databases rather than directly on the consensus chain.
It can eliminate transaction fees like a settlement clearinghouse, but it differs from a private ledger because the user's reserve is on foreign offices rather than on the domestic mint.
questions.explanation: The reading treats retail CBDCs and retail fast payment systems as related modernization tools, not identical instruments. The key distinction is the claim and settlement structure behind the user's balance.
